label: Constitutional Analysis
sentences: The question here falls under the Fourteenth Amendment. Four things in one section: people born or naturalized here and under the jurisdiction of the United States are citizens; no state may abridge the privileges or immunities of United States citizens; no state may take life, liberty or property without due process; no state may deny anyone the equal protection of the laws.
This story is about whether a state may try someone again after a jury cannot agree.

On August 17, 1789 Madison called an amendment barring the states from infringing conscience, speech, press and criminal jury trial the most valuable on the list; the House adopted it but the Senate rejected it.
The jury could not agree, so the judge declared a mistrial on 4 September.
A mistrial means she got neither a conviction nor an acquittal.
Sullivan said the deadlock created a need for mistrial, so retrial may go on.

The strongest argument against this is that this clause stops a state from again putting a person in jeopardy of life or liberty for the same offense once a trial has begun, so a second trial would take liberty without due process.
We read this clause to mean the state may not take liberty except by due process of law.
A true jury deadlock ends a trial with neither conviction nor acquittal, so a later trial is not second jeopardy.
Clear limits on when a trial may start again protect the people.

sources.label: James Madison, Remarks in Congress on the "Most Valuable Amendment," Aug. 17, 1789
